segments.title: The scenario and the five rules
sections: Right About The Market, Wrong About The Morning
Where Each Hard Rule Came From

cues.text: You marked the level. You wrote the idea. Price did what you said it would. And the session still ended worse than the read deserved.
Somewhere between 9:30 a.m. and 11 a.m., the trades stopped coming from the plan and started coming from you.
A second entry, taken because the first was easy. A stop-out answered forty seconds later. An exit, because a red candle looked big.
Your read was fine. Your morning had other plans.
That gap, between a right read and the trades you place, is what this module is about. Discipline will not close it. Discipline is what working mechanisms look like from the outside.
So every mistake here gets three things.
One: what it looks like.
Two: what it reveals about you.
Three: a mechanism that fixes it. A setting, a written line, a rehearsed routine, or a journal field.
Now, where each hard rule came from. The five rules in Module 2 look like restrictions. Each is the written answer to something traders do to themselves on a bad day.
One: the trading window. It stops the late entry taken because the level was right there.
Two: the news windows. They stop a trade turning into a bet on a number.
Three: the four reasons to flatten by hand. They stop exits on hope, on sunk cost, on a mood.
Four: the 2R kill switch, the daily loss limit you set at your broker. It stops you negotiating with your own limit.
Five: the post-loss reset. It stops the next trade coming from the last one.
The rule: keep the rules as written, and when one feels like a cost, read the behaviour it stops, not the rule.
Getting it wrong is bargaining. The window is for normal days. The reset is for big losses. It reveals you read a rule as a price, not as a decision you already made.
The fix: write what each rule stops, in your own words, on a card beside your screen, and read it aloud before the first order.
The rule does not get tired at 2:30 p.m. You do. That is the whole argument.

segments.title: Breaks and the reset
sections: The Post-Loss Reset Is A Rehearsed Skill

cues.text: A scheduled break is written on your plan before the session, at a fixed time, and taken whether the session is going well or badly.
It is never triggered by a result. A pause after a loss is a different thing, coming up next.
Attention drains with screen time, and a break at a fixed time is the cheapest repair there is. Platform closed. Away from the desk. Back to the plan, not to the last trade.
A break carries no promise. It is hygiene, like sleep. It is not a cure.
After a day or more away, the first session starts with the full pre-market routine from scratch, and one rehearsal of the reset before the first live order.
The rule: breaks sit on the plan at fixed times and are taken whatever the result.
Getting it wrong is skipping the 11 a.m. break because the morning is green. It reveals your P and L is running your breaks. The fix: an alarm for each one, and the platform closed when it rings.
Your screen will survive fifteen minutes without you. It has survived worse.
Now, the post-loss reset. It is the routine you run after every losing trade and before any new entry, and it is a skill, built by repetition in the conditions it is for.
A routine you have only run while calm, you have never run at all. After a stop-out your pulse is up, your view is narrow, and your hand is already moving toward the order ticket.
One: cancel every working entry order. A working order is the impulse, already placed.
Two: the physical step. Feet flat, one long exhale, three or four rounds of box breathing.
Three: three questions, aloud, in sentences. What is the chart telling me? Are any setups forming? What would need to happen for one to appear?
Four: write the third answer in one line in your journal. A blank line means no trade.
Once a week, with no position on, rehearse it with your heart rate up, straight after a flight of stairs or a fast walk. Count the rehearsals in the journal.
The rule: after every loss, the full reset before any new entry, rehearsed weekly.
Getting it wrong is a reset run at the screen with the chart still moving, or skipped because it was only a small loss. A reset with no rehearsals behind it is a plan, not a skill.

segments.title: The first win, and the losing run
sections: The Re-entry Loop After A First Win
Losing Is A Member Of A Distribution

cues.text: The re-entry loop is a run of entries, one after another, without a fresh setup. It usually starts after the first win of the session, not after a loss.
The first trade wins. It felt easy, and easy feels like information. The next entry comes a little faster, a little further from a level.
Nothing about the market said the second trade was better. The first trade's result did. A win is not a forecast. It is a receipt.
What protects the morning is that the second trade faces the same test as the first. Four checks, written before the order.
One: the location is a named level.
Two: the trigger fired before entry.
Three: the stop is behind structure.
Four: the size matches the plan for that stop. Two checks or fewer is a C, and a C is not taken.
The rule: every entry after the first, and especially the first after a win, gets the four checks written before the order goes in.
Getting it wrong is a second entry from mid-range, minutes after the first trade closed, with the grade filled in afterwards. That grade describes what you did. It was never a test.
Now, losing. If a read is right most of the time, the misses are not mistakes. They are the rest of the distribution.
A trade built to plan, at a named level, with a trigger and a structural stop, that hits its stop, did what the plan said it might.
Losses arrive in runs. Even when every trade is independent, over a few dozen trades a run of three in a row is the ordinary case.
Two errors sit either side of a losing run. One: reading it as a verdict, and changing the plan after three trades.
Two: reading it as nothing, when each loss carried a Broke Rule tag. That is not a distribution. That is a habit.
The rule: a plan trade that lost gets no negative tag, and setups are judged in cohorts, on the review schedule, never after a losing run.
Getting it wrong is tagging a plan loss as a bad entry. It reveals you are grading outcomes. Tag at the exit from the four checks and the four flatten reasons, never from the R column.

segments.title: Curious or needing, and the only failure

cues.text: There are two ways to sit down in front of a chart. Curious: you want to see what the market does at your levels, and you would be content to watch it do something you cannot trade.
Needing: you want something from the session. A green day, a loss repaid, being right about an earlier idea, or just something to happen.
The market is the same either way. What you see in it is not. Boredom is not a setup. It only dresses like one.
The readiness score puts a number on it, from 0 to 2, at the top of your pre-market sheet.
2: curious about what the market does at your levels.
1: neutral.
0: needing something from the market.
It is data for your journal, not a gate. A completed sheet clears you to trade, whatever the score.
The rule: score yourself honestly every morning, and use the score as data in the review, never as a permission or a ban in the session.
Getting it wrong is scoring a 2 every day because a 0 feels like failing, or acting on it. A measurement that is managed stops measuring. The score never touches size.
Now, the only failure. On this course, a trade lost is not a failure. A rule broken is, whether the trade made money or not.
The winning rule-break is the dangerous one. A trade from mid-range that happens to work pays you for the thing you are trying to stop, and that pay is the strongest training signal there is.
That is why a winning C is a warning, not a result, and why a Broke Rule tag stays on a winner.
It also means the failure is in your control. You cannot decide whether the next trade wins. You can decide whether it was taken by the plan.
The rule: a rule broken is tagged whatever the result, and the count of broken rules is the first number of every weekly review.
Getting it wrong is leaving the tag off a winner. The fix is a ledger: every tagged trade, winners first, with its R and the rule it broke, totalled in R and never netted against plan trades.

segments.title: The mechanical fixes and the worked case
sections: The Mechanical Fixes, In One List
Worked Case: The Morning After The First Win

cues.text: Now, the mechanical fixes, in one list. Each is a setting, a written line, a rehearsal or a journal field. None is a resolution to try harder. Trying harder is a wish with a gym membership.
Bargaining or trading past 2R: the card by your screen, and the limit set at the account with the lock on.
Exiting on a mood: one of the four reasons, or a Too Early tag.
Skipped breaks and cold returns: an alarm for each break, and a return-day line on the plan.
Re-entry and a reset that never runs: the written third answer, and a weekly rehearsal.
The second trade after a win: the grade line, written before the order.
Forgiving a winning rule-break: the ledger, never netted.
What is not on the list is deliberate. No cap on trades, no stop after a loss count, no smaller size after a red day. The 2R kill switch is the cap, and base R is fixed.
The rule: losing trades are the cost of a plan, and broken rules are the only failure.
Now, the example. A composite morning, invented prices, built to show the fixes working in order. It belongs to no one, and it is not a trade record.
At 9:22 a.m. the sheet carries two branches, one long, one short, and a nothing case. The last line is a readiness score, with one line why. Nothing about the plan changes because of it.

At 9:58 a.m., a second long looks easy from mid-range. The grade line comes first. Location, mid-range. Trigger, none. Stop, nothing to put it behind. That is a C. It is written, not taken, and no order goes in.
At 10:22 a.m. the other branch fires. The grade line is written before the order, and the trade is built to plan, so whatever it does, it carries no negative tag.

After a loss, the reset runs. Orders cancelled, feet flat, one long exhale, three questions aloud, the third answer written. Then the 11 a.m. alarm. The break is on the plan, so it is taken on a green morning exactly as on a red one.

Notice what decided the morning. The read was the same in both versions. Two moments mattered: a written line before an order never placed, and a routine after a loss that sent the next trade back to the chart.

cues.text: Which of these is yours? Answer from your journal, not from memory, for your last ten sessions or as many as you have. One point for each line that is true.
One: every entry after a loss has a written third answer, timestamped before it.
Two: you rehearsed the reset with your heart rate up in each of the last two weeks.
Three: no trade at grade C, and every grade line written before its order.
Four: no losing A+ or A trade carries a negative tag.
Five: every plan had its breaks written, and every break was taken.
Six: a readiness score for every session, and no size changed because of it.

Six of six: the mechanisms are in place, and the weekly review keeps them there. Four or five: the first false line is next week's one fix, and only that one. Under four: fix line one before your next session, and add the others one a week.
One line overrides the score. If line one is false, it is the fix, whatever the total, because every other line depends on the next trade coming from the chart.
Your assignment. Run the post-loss reset once, with no position on, straight after a flight of stairs or a fast two-minute walk.

Cancel orders on an empty ticket. Feet flat, one long exhale, four rounds of box breathing. The three questions aloud. Then write the third answer in your journal, with the time. That is the whole assignment.
Where it goes next. Every mechanism here lands in the journal.
Module 18, Journaling and Review, teaches the tags and the weekly review where the ledger lives.
Module 16 puts the readiness score on the sheet, and Module 17 covers the hours between the open and the close.
Module 19 holds the daily habits, and Module 21 teaches how to read a distribution from your own record.
You marked the level. Now the morning follows the plan. The chart can keep its opinions.

check.q: Where do you answer the six lines from?
options: Your journal, for your last ten sessions
check.why: Answer from the journal, because memory agrees with how the day ended.

check.q: Your score is 5. What do you do?
options: Fix every false line at once
Fix the first false line next week, and only that one
check.why: Four or five means one fix at a time, starting with the first false line.

check.q: Line one is false and the total is 5 of 6. What happens?
options: Line one is still the fix
check.why: Line one overrides the score because every other line depends on the next trade coming from the chart.

check.q: What does the assignment have you rehearse?
options: The post-loss reset, with your heart rate up and no position on
check.why: You practise the routine in a body that resembles the one you will be in when it matters.

questions.q: Which best describes discipline in this module?
options: A supply you spend through the session
What a working set of mechanisms looks like from the outside
A trait that fades with age
questions.why: Every mistake gets a mechanism: a setting, a written line, a rehearsal or a journal field.

questions.q: What is the first step of the post-loss reset?
questions.why: A working order is the impulse already placed, so entry orders go first.

questions.q: A break is skipped because the morning is green. What does that reveal?
options: Your P and L is running your breaks
questions.why: Breaks are set at fixed times and taken whatever the result.

questions.q: Why does the re-entry loop begin after a win?
options: The first win is read as information about the next trade
The market turns after a win
questions.why: Nothing about the market said the second trade was better. The first result did.

questions.q: A plan trade hits its stop. Which tag does it get?
questions.why: A trade built and exited to plan that lost carries no negative tag.

questions.q: What does the readiness score do?
questions.why: It is data, never a permission or a ban, and it never touches size.

questions.q: Which is the only failure counted on this course?
options: A rule broken, whatever the result
questions.why: A winning rule-break is the dangerous one, so the tag stays on a winner.

questions.q: What is the first number of every weekly review?
questions.why: The ledger counts broken rules first, then totals their R, and never nets them against plan trades.
